pos: n. (Fife burgh, archbishopric and university; where Patrick Hamilton and George Wishart were burned)
etymology: Named for the apostle Andrew, whose relics the medieval see claimed; earlier Gaelic Cennrigmonaid.
biblical_def: St Andrews was the ecclesiastical capital of Scotland and the place where the Scottish Reformation was paid for. Patrick Hamilton, a young abbot of noble birth who had studied at Wittenberg, was burned before the gate of St Salvator's College in February 1528 and took six hours to die; the proverb that the reek of Master Patrick Hamilton infected all it blew upon was coined by a Catholic who had watched. George Wishart was burned in front of the castle in March 1546 with Cardinal Beaton watching from a window; Beaton was murdered in that castle three months later, and John Knox, who had carried Wishart's two-handed sword, preached his first sermon in the parish church in 1547. Andrew Melville afterwards made St Mary's College the seminary of Presbyterian Scotland. The dictionary records St Andrews because the burnings were not incidental to the Scottish Reformation; they were its seed. “if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death in defence of the truth, particularly of the Christian faith, testimony as a solemn declaration made for proving some fact, and a stake as a piece of timber set in the ground.
webster_full: MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the truth, particularly of the Christian faith.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
STAKE, n. A small piece of wood or timber, sharpened at one end and set in the ground, or prepared for setting, as for a fence.
SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species; offspring; progeny.

Act 7:60

corruption_summary: Scotland's archbishopric, where Hamilton burned in 1528 and Wishart in 1546, and where Knox first preached in 1547.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern instinct to treat the martyrs as victims of an age of intolerance, which turns their deaths into an argument for not holding anything too firmly. They died because they held something firmly, and the Scottish church they left behind did the same.

The principle to recover is that the death of the faithful is fruitful by God's appointment and not by accident. The Lord states the law of it in agricultural terms: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24). The victory is won by testimony and by a willingness to lose: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). The catalogue of such deaths is already in Scripture — “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword” (Heb 11:37) — and the manner of dying is given by Stephen: “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge” (Act 7:60).

pos: n. (Angus burgh on the Tay; the first Scottish town to receive the Reformation, called the Scottish Geneva)
etymology: From Gaelic Dun Deagh, the fort on the Tay; Scots Dundee.
biblical_def: Dundee was the earliest and most thoroughly reformed of the Scottish burghs, and its neighbours called it the Scottish Geneva. Reformed preaching was heard there in the 1520s, the burgh council was evangelical a generation before the Reformation Parliament of 1560, and the town supplied men and money to every stage of the cause. Its great contribution was a songbook: the brothers James, John and Robert Wedderburn, of a Dundee merchant family, compiled the Gude and Godlie Ballatis, metrical psalms and vernacular spiritual songs in broad Scots, some of them reworkings of popular tunes, which carried the doctrines of grace into households that owned no books. The dictionary records Dundee because singing is how a reformation reaches the illiterate and the young. “Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints” (Psa 149:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalm as a sacred song designed to be sung in the worship of God, melody as an agreeable succession of sounds, and praise as the expression of gratitude for favours conferred.
webster_full: PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition designed to be sung in the worship of God.
MEL'ODY, n. An agreeable succession of sounds; a tune.
PRAISE, n. Commendation bestowed on a person for his personal virtues or worthy actions; the expression of gratitude for personal favors conferred.
SONG, n. In general, that which is sung or uttered with musical modulations of the voice, whether of the human voice or that of a bird.

A Psalm. O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory.
Eph 5:19

Psa 47:7

corruption_summary: The first Scottish burgh to reform, and the home of the Wedderburns' Gude and Godlie Ballatis.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the treatment of congregational singing as the warm-up to the sermon, chosen for mood, rather than as the people's own confession set to a tune they will still be humming on a Tuesday. The Wedderburns knew what they were doing: doctrine in Scots, to tunes already in every mouth.

The principle to recover is that praise is commanded, congregational, and intelligent. The call is to the gathered church: “Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints” (Psa 149:1). The ground of the song is what God has done: “O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things” (Psa 98:1). Its content is to pass between the people as well as upward: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19). And it must engage the mind: “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7).

pos: n. (royal burgh and castle on the Forth; where Knox preached in 1559 and the Scottish lords banded)
etymology: From an uncertain Brittonic root, perhaps Striveling, the place of strife; Scots Stirling.
biblical_def: Stirling guarded the one road between the Lowlands and the Highlands, and whoever held its castle held Scotland. The Reformation turned on it twice: John Knox preached in the Church of the Holy Rude in 1559 after the Lords of the Congregation had been driven back from Edinburgh, and his sermon on the covenant and the people's failures reportedly restored a collapsing cause in a single hour; and in 1567 the infant James VI was crowned in that church, with a Protestant sermon and no mass, which settled the succession for the Reformed religion. The castle also saw the bands and covenants by which the Scottish nobility bound themselves to each other and to the cause. The dictionary records Stirling because the Scottish habit of binding by written covenant, which produced the National Covenant of 1638, has a biblical warrant it rarely gets credit for: “And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a band as a company of persons united in a common design, an oath as a solemn declaration made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed, and a covenanter in Scottish history as one who subscribed the national covenant.
webster_full: BAND, n. A company of persons united in any common design; a body of armed men.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
COV'ENANTER, n. One who makes a covenant. In Scottish history, one who subscribed the national covenant.
STAT'UTE, n. An act of the legislature of a state that extends its binding force to all the citizens or subjects of that state; a written law.

corruption_summary: Knox in the Holy Rude in 1559, the coronation of James VI in 1567, and the banding of the Scottish lords.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern discomfort with corporate religious oaths, which are read as presumptuous, coercive or quaint. Scotland's covenants had real faults and the practice itself is scriptural: a people may bind itself, in writing, before God, to keep His commandments.

The principle to recover is that public covenanting is a biblical act with a biblical form — written, read aloud, subscribed, and binding. Josiah's renewal is the model, and the people were party to it: “And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3). Joshua did the same with a statute attached: “So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem” (Jos 24:25). Jehoiada bound ruler and people together: “that they should be the LORD'S people” (2Ch 23:16). And Nehemiah's generation subscribed it with their names: they “entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law” (Neh 10:29).

pos: n. (burgh and university of the north-east; home of the Aberdeen Doctors who refused the National Covenant)
etymology: From Gaelic Aberdeon, the mouth of the Don; Scots Aberdeen.
biblical_def: Aberdeen was the one substantial Scottish city that would not sign. When the National Covenant was subscribed across the kingdom in 1638, the divines of King's College and Marischal College — John Forbes of Corse, Robert Baron, William Leslie, James Sibbald and others, known as the Aberdeen Doctors — published a reasoned refusal: they held episcopacy and the ceremonies to be things not commanded and not forbidden, and so denied that a man could be bound by oath to reject them as sinful. The Covenanters answered them in print and then with troops. The dictionary holds that the Doctors were wrong on the substance — the regulative principle leaves no room for a worship ordinance that Scripture has not commanded — and that the Covenanters were wrong to settle the argument by force. “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5) does not make the question indifferent; it does mean a conscience is not changed by a garrison.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions, a scruple as hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right, and liberty as freedom from restraint.
webster_full: CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
SCRUPLE, n. Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
scriptures: Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other: for why is my liberty judged of another man's conscience?
And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.
corruption_summary: The Aberdeen Doctors' reasoned refusal of the National Covenant in 1638, answered first in print and then with troops.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs both ways, and Aberdeen caught both. One error treats disputed ceremonies as indifferent when Scripture has in fact spoken, which is the Doctors' error on episcopacy and the ceremonies. The other treats a sworn conscience as something a majority may overrule by force, which is what was done to them.

The principle to recover is that conscience is bound by Scripture and by nothing else, and that a man acting against his own persuasion sins even when the thing itself is lawful. Paul requires settled persuasion: “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5). Acting against it is condemned: “he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23). My liberty is not the measure of another man's scruple, nor his of mine: “why is my liberty judged of another man's conscience?” (1Co 10:29). And the apostolic aim is a conscience clear before both courts: “to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men” (Act 24:16).

pos: n. (royal burgh and palace in West Lothian; where the Covenants were publicly burned in 1662)
etymology: From Brittonic llyn llaith cau, the lake in the damp hollow; Scots Linlithgow.
biblical_def: Linlithgow was a royal burgh with a palace, and in the Restoration it became the stage for a deliberate act of contempt. On the twenty-ninth of May 1662, the anniversary of Charles II's return, the magistrates and the episcopal party of the burgh staged an elaborate public spectacle in which the National Covenant, the Solemn League and Covenant and the acts of the Reformed General Assemblies were carried in mock procession and burned in the street, with the figure of a Whig on top. It was answered by Scotland's twenty-eight years of field preaching and killing times. The dictionary records the burning because Scripture has an exact precedent for it, and the precedent includes the sequel: Jehoiakim cut up the roll and cast it into the fire, and the word of the LORD came again to Jeremiah: “Take thee again another roll” (Jer 36:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a roll as a register or official list of names, a scribe in Scripture as a writer and a doctor of the law, and a band as a company of persons united in a common design.
webster_full: ROLL, n. A register; a catalogue or official list of names.
SCRIBE, n. In Scripture and the Jewish history, a clerk or secretary to the king; also, a writer and a doctor of the law.
BAND, n. A company of persons united in any common design; a body of armed men.
COV'ENANTER, n. One who makes a covenant. In Scottish history, one who subscribed the national covenant.

corruption_summary: The public burning of the Covenants and the acts of the Reformed Assemblies in the burgh street, May 1662.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a state can end a doctrine by destroying its documents, or that ridicule disposes of a conviction. Linlithgow burned the Covenants with a good deal of wit, and the men who held them went to the hills and preached for a generation.

The principle to recover is that the word of God survives its burning and comes back larger. The act is recorded without flinching: Jehoiakim's servant “cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed” (Jer 36:23). The reply is immediate: “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll” (Jer 36:28). And the second edition is longer than the first: “there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jer 36:32). The psalm has already named the spirit of such ceremonies: “Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us” (Psa 2:3).

pos: n. (Fife royal burgh and abbey; the abbey stripped at the Reformation in 1560)
etymology: From Gaelic Dun Fearnmhalin, perhaps the fort by the crooked stream; Scots Dunfermline.
biblical_def: Dunfermline was the burial place of the Scottish kings and the richest Benedictine house in the kingdom, and in March 1560 a party from the reforming lords went through it and destroyed the altars, the images and the shrine of Queen Margaret. The nave survived and became the parish church, where it still stands with Robert the Bruce buried under the choir. The dictionary records Dunfermline because the removal of images is the hardest thing in the Scottish Reformation for a modern reader to forgive, and the dictionary does not apologise for it. The second commandment is not a matter of taste, and the kings of Judah whom Scripture commends are commended for exactly this work: Hezekiah “removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves” (2Ki 18:4). What deserves blame at Dunfermline is not the obedience but the disorder of it — mobs, not magistrates, and good building destroyed with the idols.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an image as a representation of any person or thing formed of a material substance, an idol as an image consecrated as an object of worship, and a grove in Scripture as the rendering of the Hebrew asherah, a wooden image set up beside an altar.
webster_full: IMAGE, n. [L. imago.] A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; an idol.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
GROVE, n. In Scripture, the rendering of the Hebrew asherah, a wooden image or symbol set up beside an altar in idolatrous worship.
SANCTUARY, n. [L. sanctuarium, from sanctus, sacred.] A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, called the Holy of Holies.

corruption_summary: Scotland's richest abbey and royal mausoleum, stripped of its altars, images and shrine in March 1560.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the modern treatment of the second commandment as a cultural preference, so that images in worship are discussed as a matter of heritage, beauty or sensibility, and the commandment itself is quietly reclassified as an Old Testament severity the church has outgrown. Rome, Orthodoxy and a growing body of evangelical practice all do this, each for different reasons.

The principle to recover is that God forbids images in His worship and commends those who remove them. The commandment is plain: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). Hezekiah's reform is recorded as praise: he “removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves” (2Ki 18:4). The command to Israel entering the land was thorough: “ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves” (Deu 7:5). And the people did it themselves in Hezekiah's day: they “brake the images in pieces, and cut down the groves, and threw down the high places” (2Ch 31:1).

pos: n. (Fife burgh on the Forth, the lang toun; a Reformed salt and shipping town)
etymology: From Brittonic caer caled din, the fort on the hard hill, later read as the Scots kirk.
biblical_def: Kirkcaldy was a long single street of salt pans, coal heughs and shipmasters' houses along the Forth, and it reformed with the rest of Fife in 1560. It has no martyr and no synod; what it has is the ordinary Scottish parish of the century after the Reformation, in which the kirk session minuted the discipline of its members week by week, the elders visited, the heads of households were examined before communion, and family worship morning and evening was expected of every house and enquired into when it was not kept. The dictionary records Kirkcaldy as the type of that ordinary godliness, because the Scottish Reformation's real achievement was not its battles but its households. “I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2) is the resolution, and the New Testament makes the government of a man's own house the test of his fitness to govern in the church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a household as those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family, a family as the collective body of persons who live in one house under one head, and a burgh as a corporate town with certain privileges.
webster_full: HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; a family living together.
FAMILY, n. The collective body of persons who live in one house and under one head; a race; a clan.
BURGH, n. A borough; a corporate town or village with certain privileges.
ELDER, n. One who is older; in Scripture, a person who on account of age is selected to be a ruler or officer.

One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;

corruption_summary: An ordinary reformed Fife burgh: kirk session discipline, elders' visitation, and family worship enquired into.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern privacy of the household, which makes the state of a family's worship nobody's business but its own, and so removes it from the only oversight that was ever likely to sustain it. The Scottish elders asked, and the asking is why it lasted.

The principle to recover is that the household is a unit of worship and of oversight, and that a man's rule of his own house is a public qualification. The psalmist makes it a resolution: “I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2). The eldership requires it: “One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity” (1Ti 3:4). Cornelius is commended by household: “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house” (Act 10:2). And the LORD names it as the reason He chose Abraham: “he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD” (Gen 18:19).

pos: n. (Angus burgh; where Greek was first taught in Scotland, under John Erskine of Dun)
etymology: From Gaelic Monadh Rois, the moor of the promontory; Scots Montrose.
biblical_def: Montrose made one contribution to the Scottish Reformation that no other burgh could claim. John Erskine of Dun, its laird and later superintendent of Angus and Mearns, brought a Frenchman named Pierre de Marsilliers to the town about 1534 and set him to teach Greek, the first regular teaching of the language in Scotland; among those who learned it there was George Wishart, who afterwards read the Greek New Testament to his hearers and was burned for it. Erskine himself was four times Moderator of the General Assembly and the one man trusted by both Knox and the Regent. The dictionary records Montrose because a Reformation stands or falls on access to the text in the tongue it was written in, and in Scotland that access began in a small east-coast burgh with one hired master. “Buy the truth, and sell it not” (Pro 23:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines certainty as a full assurance of mind and exemption from doubt, truth as conformity to fact or reality, and a tittle as a small particle, a minute part, a jot.
webster_full: CERTAIN'TY, n. A full assurance of mind; exemption from doubt.
TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
TIT'TLE, n. A small particle; a minute part; a jot; an iota.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; the power of articulate utterance.
scriptures: Luk 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Mat 5:18
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
corruption_summary: Where Erskine of Dun had Greek taught from about 1534, the first in Scotland, and where Wishart learned it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that the original languages are a specialism for scholars rather than the ordinary equipment of a preacher, which leaves a congregation entirely dependent on whichever English version its minister happens to prefer and unable to weigh a disputed rendering at all.

The principle to recover is that certainty about what is written is the object, and that it is worth paying for. Luke states his purpose in writing: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4). The proverb puts truth in the language of purchase, bought at a price and never sold: “Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding” (Pro 23:23). The text itself is refined and exact: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6). And the smallest marks of it are guaranteed: “one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law” (Mat 5:18).

pos: n. (royal burgh of the south-west; the market town of the Covenanting country)
etymology: From Gaelic Dun Phris, the fort of the thicket; Scots Dumfries.
biblical_def: Dumfries was the capital of the Scottish south-west, and the south-west was where the Covenant held longest. After the Restoration the ejected ministers of Galloway, Nithsdale and Annandale preached in the open country rather than conform, and from 1663 attending such a meeting was a crime and keeping one a capital one; dragoons were quartered on the parishes, fines ruined the tenantry, and the Killing Times of the 1680s took their victims from these moors. The declaration that opened the rising of 1666 was published at Dumfries. The dictionary records the burgh and its hinterland because field preaching is the clearest case in church history of a church reduced to nothing but the word and a hillside, and still a church. “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to preach as to proclaim and to inculcate publicly by argument or exhortation, a congregation as a collection or assembly, and a shepherd as a man employed in tending and guarding sheep in the field.
webster_full: PREACH, v.t. To proclaim; to publish in religious discourse; to inculcate publicly by argument or exhortation.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; the whole body of the people of Israel.
SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the field.
SABBATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employments, and to be kept holy and consecrated to his service and worship.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
And on the sabbath we went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made; and we sat down, and spake unto the women which resorted thither.

As a shepherd seeketh out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered; so will I seek out my sheep, and will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: The market town of the Covenanting south-west, where the rising of 1666 was declared and the Killing Times fell.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of the church with its building and its legal standing, so that a congregation which loses both is assumed to have ceased. The Covenanters lost their pulpits, their stipends, their legal existence and in many cases their lives, and held communion seasons on open moors with thousands present.

The principle to recover is that the church is constituted by Christ's presence among His gathered people and not by its premises. The promise is given to the smallest gathering: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20). The apostolic precedent is a riverside: “on the sabbath we went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made” (Act 16:13). The scattered flock is sought by the Shepherd Himself: “so will I seek out my sheep, and will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered” (Eze 34:12). And the charge to the minister does not depend on circumstances: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (Ayrshire burgh; David Dickson's ministry and the Stewarton revival of the 1620s)
etymology: From Brittonic Irfon, perhaps the fresh or green river; Scots Irvine.
biblical_def: Irvine was David Dickson's parish, and from it came one of the first recorded revivals in Scotland. Dickson was settled there in 1618, was banished for a time for refusing the Articles of Perth, and returned; from about 1625 his Monday market-day sermons drew people from the whole of north Ayrshire, and the work spread into the neighbouring parish of Stewarton so that it was called, half in mockery, the Stewarton sickness, from the weeping and the distress of conscience under the preaching. Dickson went on to the Glasgow and Edinburgh chairs and to the writing of the Sum of Saving Knowledge. The dictionary records Irvine because this is what the Scriptures describe when a congregation is actually convicted, and the mockers' name for it was more accurate than they knew: “they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?” (Act 2:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revival as return or recovery to life from death or apparent death, to revive as to return to life, to mourn as to grieve and lament, and supplication as humble and earnest prayer in worship.
webster_full: REVI'VAL, n. Return, recall or recovery to life from death or apparent death.
REVIVE, v.i. To return to life; to recover life.
MOURN, v.i. To grieve; to lament; to sorrow; to wear the customary habit of sorrow.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship.
scriptures: Act 2:37
Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?

And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Hab 3:2
O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.
corruption_summary: David Dickson's market-day preaching from 1625 and the Stewarton revival, mocked as a sickness.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption here is revivalism, which takes the effects God sometimes gives and attempts to produce them by technique: the extended appeal, the engineered atmosphere, the measured decision. Dickson preached the ordinary doctrines on a market day and the work came; he did not know how to make it come, and never claimed to.

The principle to recover is that conviction of sin is the Spirit's work under the preached word, and that it is to be prayed for rather than manufactured. Pentecost describes the effect exactly: “they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?” (Act 2:37). The prophet traces it to a divine outpouring: “I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications” (Zec 12:10), and names the effect: “they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him” (Zec 12:10). The church is taught to ask for it: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6), and “O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years” (Hab 3:2).
